title: Hybrid latency/cost batching regulator for mixed prompt/response workloads
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Background: Production traffic shows a heavy mixture of short prompts (1-16 tokens) followed by long responses (200-1200 tokens) for chat-style workloads. Our current continuous-batcher defaults to a static aggressiveness parameter which yields either low latency for short-turn-first traffic or good unit-cost for long-response dominated traffic, but not both. This ticket implements a hybrid regulator that dynamically reconciles per-tenant SLA targets (p50/p95 latency) with unit-cost objectives by adjusting batching aggressiveness and KV residency budgets per slot in real time.
approach: 1) Observation model: use a lightweight horizon estimator that classifies incoming requests into short/medium/long-turn distributions over a 30s sliding window per-customer and per-route. 2) Controller: implement a PID-style regulator with a cost term (tokens/sec efficiency) and a latency term (measured p95 tail). The controller computes a scalar aggressiveness multiplier and a KV-residency target which are fed into the existing continuous-batcher. 3) Safeguards: per-tenant hard SLO clamps, monotonic backoff on KV reclamation to avoid cache storms, and a hysteresis layer to prevent flip-flopping. 4) Learning-based augmentation (experimental): log features for an RL policy offline; initial rollout uses rule-based controller and a simulated replay environment for policy training.
implementation_notes: - New component: batch-regulator service (stateless, runs alongside scheduler) exposes gRPC/HTTP endpoint for updates. - Add two config knobs to batcher: aggressiveness_multiplier and kv_residency_target. - Use existing KV metrics (kv_hit_ratio, kv_eviction_rate, kv_resident_bytes) and latency histograms. - Keep regulator decisions idempotent and versioned for safe rollback. - Metric tagging: decisions are tagged by customer_id, route, and controller_version.
metrics_and_targets: Primary metrics: p50 latency (ms), p95 latency (ms), tokens/sec per-GPU, token cost ($/1k tokens). Targets for canary: p95 <= 600ms for short-turn routes, <1200ms for mixed routes; tokens/sec improvement >= 8% vs baseline when traffic has >30% long responses while p95 degradation <= 5% for short-turn-only routes. KV hit ratio should not drop more than 4 percentage points in steady-state.
test_plan: Unit tests for regulator math and boundary conditions. Integration tests with continuous-batcher simulation harness (replay production traces with mixlen labels). Canary rollout: 1) internal canary traffic (synthetic mixes) -> 2) 1% real traffic on a dedicated pool with canary flag -> 3) 10% after 48h stability -> full. Add automated rollback if p95 regresses >10% or token cost rises >15% for 1h.
acceptance_criteria: - Regulator deploys to staging and runs for 72h against replayed week-of-traffic. - Canary shows tokens/sec improvement >=8% in long-response heavy traces without p95 >1200ms. - No customer observed KV storms during canary; kv_eviction_rate spikes limited to <2x baseline. - Rollout playbook (steps + rollback triggers) documented and reviewed by SRE and PM.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: aggressive KV reclamation could cause cache churn and latency spikes. Mitigation: enforce monotonic reclaim smoothing and a minimum residency floor per customer. Risk: oscillation between latency/cost objectives. Mitigation: add hysteresis and derivative damping to the regulator. Risk: added regulator latency in control loop. Mitigation: keep controller compute <2ms and run decisions at 100-500ms cadence (configurable).
